source_neutral.procedure: The procedure assumes, without supporting facts supplied in the packet, that the surviving draft can be divided into units with physically secured internal leaf order, and that changing working conditions leave corresponding features on materials the author worked on during a given period. Some units are assumed to have date anchors from dated witnesses or correspondence referring to identifiable passages or materials; other units have uncertain positions in composition time. Record leaf order and material and textual features, distinguish revision layers, construct a reference sequence from anchored units, and compare the ordered feature transitions of units to identify candidate relative positions. Examine localized discrepancies for missing or inserted leaves, test alignments by withholding feature classes, and examine features spanning units for evidence of assembly. Narrative position is not evidence of composition position. Without an anchored unit, the attainable result is a relative sequence without an absolute date anchor.
source_neutral.action: 1. Segment the draft into gatherings, notebook sections, typescript runs, inserted leaves or slips, or other units whose internal leaf order is secured by conjugate leaves, text continuing across page breaks, or original foliation. Record that order independently of narrative order. 2. Using a fixed written protocol, record the state of each feature class for every leaf in every unit: paper, ink or writing instrument, pagination scheme, character and place name forms, and hand. Record overlying revision layers as separate series from the base text. Complete recording before attempting alignment. 3. Build the reference sequence exclusively from anchored units. 4. Compare each unit without a date anchor with the reference and with other units without date anchors at successive leaf offsets. Record every offset at which the order of feature transitions corresponds between units. 5. At each candidate offset, test whether correspondence holds on both sides of a point but is displaced by one or more leaves. At such points, propose a missing or inserted leaf, then check separately for physical evidence: stubs, foliation gaps, broken textual continuity, offset ink, or differing paper stock. 6. Repeat alignment with one feature class held out to determine whether the remaining classes recover the same offset. 7. Examine features spanning units, such as a single pagination run or uniform corrections in later ink, as a separate series bearing on assembly rather than composition.
source_neutral.observables: Recorded features include paper stock, ruling or watermark; ink, writing instrument or typewriter characteristics; pagination scheme; forms of character and place names; and features of the hand. Supporting observations would consist of a single offset per unit at which several independently recorded feature classes change in corresponding order across two or more units and against the anchored reference, with that offset recovered when any one feature class is withheld. Further support would consist of remaining mismatches localized at specific points that coincide with separately observed physical evidence of removed or inserted leaves. An assembly observation would be a feature, such as continuous pagination or one correcting ink, extending across units whose base features align to different composition positions. Non-supporting observations would include several equally fitting offsets, feature classes indicating different offsets, a proposed gap without a physical trace, or an anchored date contradicting the aligned position.
source_neutral.inferential_warrant: Consistent alignment would support a relative composition order for units and revision layers distinct from narrative order, placement within that order of units previously lacking a position, and identification of specific points where a leaf is probably missing or was inserted later. Alignment involving anchored units would support bounded date ranges rather than precise dates. Features applied across units with different composition positions would support a later assembly stage at which those units were brought together. The result is a ranked sequence hypothesis retained alongside alternatives. Uncertain claims include the placement of units meeting the stopping conditions; absolute dates when anchors are absent or doubtful; the content and number of lost witnesses; whether a leaf is a fair copy whose material features date copying rather than composition; and the time interval between adjacent sequence positions.
source_neutral.problem_decomposition: The draft is divided into units with internally secured leaf order. Each leaf and each revision layer on a leaf, including base text, later insertions and deletions, is treated as a separate element in the comparison. Revision layers form series distinct from base-text series. Units are distinguished by whether they have date anchors. Ordered feature transitions connect units through candidate leaf offsets, while features spanning units are considered separately as evidence about assembly. The assumed relationship is that working conditions changing over composition time mark whatever the author writes during that period. Leaves may be missing through removal or loss, added through later insertion, or misassigned through renumbering, recopying or reordering by the author or a later archive. Composition order, narrative order and assembly sequence are treated separately.
source_neutral.next_inquiry: For units left unplaced, collate further witnesses, re-inspect material features, and consult dated correspondence or provenance records. All named features and anchors remain assumptions requiring confirmation on the documents because the packet supplies no facts about the particular draft.
source_neutral.limits: Do not assign a position to a unit if its overlap with other units contains fewer than two distinct transitions, if its pattern is uniform or repeats, or if feature classes favor different offsets. Record the unit as unplaced and retain competing sequences. Local changes, such as a borrowed pen, travel or a stray sheet of old stock, can imitate or mask a transition. Correspondence between feature sequences may be weak when the author uses several inks or stocks concurrently, returns to earlier materials, or alternates work among units. Short units and drafts on uniform materials can produce short or repetitive patterns fitting many offsets. Recording hand and ink involves observer error and judgment. Anchors can be wrong because of misdated letters or later archival dating, and overlap between units may be insufficient. Leaves do not represent equal durations or fixed annual intervals. Their features have a limited number of discrete states and are under the author's control rather than necessarily determined by external conditions; these properties increase the possibility of chance agreement. No validated statistical threshold for an acceptable match is assumed. Paper stock supplies an earliest possible date, since use can occur long after acquisition. Recopying places earlier text on later material, so text and substrate may date from different times. Archival reordering or rebinding may have altered the physical order used for segmentation. If a unit's order was established using the same features used for alignment, the alignment is circular for that unit. Without an anchored unit, the sequence cannot be assigned absolute dates. Every feature and anchor named requires confirmation on the documents.
